pos: a. (glad; gladsome; causing or full of joy)
etymology: From joy, Old French joie, from Latin gaudium, gladness, from gaudere, to rejoice. The Authorized Version uses it twice over: of a city loud with mirth, and of the chastening that does not seem joyous.
biblical_def: Joyous in the Authorized Version is a word with two faces. Three times it describes a city: “Thou that art full of stirs, a tumultuous city, a joyous city: thy slain men are not slain with the sword” (Isa 22:2), and “Is this your joyous city, whose antiquity is of ancient days?” (Isa 23:7). In both places the joy is the last noise a doomed people make. Jerusalem is joyous on the day her walls are being measured for the breach; Tyre is joyous with the wealth of the sea in her lap and her exile already written. The fourth use turns the word inside out: “Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby” (Heb 12:11). Notice the verb. It does not say chastening is not joyous; it says it seemeth not to be. The rod in a Father's hand is doing a glad work under a grievous feeling, because “whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth” (Heb 12:6). So Scripture sets two joys side by side and tells the believer to prefer the one that hurts. The joyous city is merry and perishing. The chastened son is weeping and being saved. A man who cannot tell these apart will spend his life chasing the wrong gladness.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines joyous as glad; gay; merry; joyful; giving joy.
webster_full: JOY'OUS, a. [Fr. joyeux.]
1. Glad; gay; merry; joyful; noting the temper or disposition; as a joyous youth.
2. Giving joy; as joyous news.
3. Happy; as the joyous days of peace.
In Scripture the word is applied both to the merriment of a city under judgment and, negatively, to chastening, which seemeth not to be joyous for the present.
scriptures: Hebrews 12:11
Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby.
Isaiah 22:2
Thou that art full of stirs, a tumultuous city, a joyous city: thy slain men are not slain with the sword, nor dead in battle.
Isaiah 23:7
Is this your joyous city, whose antiquity is of ancient days? her own feet shall carry her afar off to sojourn.
Hebrews 12:6
For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth.
corruption_summary: The age has kept the word joyous and thrown away the chastening that makes joy honest.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern religion has made joyous a mood to be produced rather than a fruit to be grown. The worship hour is engineered for it, the sermon is measured by it, and the believer who is not feeling it is quietly counted a problem. Hebrews 12:11 cuts across the whole apparatus. It grants outright that the Father's dealing does not seem joyous. The man under the rod is not failing; he is being farmed. To demand a joyous face from a chastened son is to call the Father's ordinary method a defect.

The opposite error is the joyous city. Isaiah's two towns are loud, prosperous, and doomed, and neither of them knows it. That is the more dangerous counterfeit, because it feels exactly like blessing. A church can be full of stirs and still be Isaiah 22. The test is not the volume of the gladness but whether the gladness can survive the rod. Joy that dies the moment God says no was never the peaceable fruit of righteousness; it was the noise of a city.
roots_summary: Greek chara (G5479), joy; Hebrew 'alliz (H5947), exultant, jubilant; Latin gaudium, gladness.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'alliz (H5947) — exultant, rejoicing; the word behind the joyous city of Isaiah 22:2 and 23:7.
Greek chara (G5479) — joy; Hebrews 12:11 says chastening seemeth not to be of this kind, not that it is not.
Greek dokei (G1380) — it seems; the hinge of Hebrews 12:11, placing the grief in the appearance and the joy in the outcome.
Latin gaudium — gladness, the root Webster traces through French joyeux.
Greek karpon eirenikon (G2590, G1516) — peaceable fruit; the afterward that makes the chastening joyous in fact.
usage: “A tumultuous city, a joyous city” — Isaiah's mirth on the eve of the breach.
“Seemeth to be joyous” — the chastening only seems otherwise; the fruit is peaceable.
“Whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth” — the rod is the proof of sonship, not its absence.

pos: adv. (in a glorious manner; splendidly; with triumph)
etymology: From glorious, Latin gloriosus, from gloria, glory, renown, praise. The adverb appears three times in the Authorized Version, twice in the same song and once at the end of the world.
biblical_def: Gloriously is a word the Bible reserves for what God does, never for what man achieves. Its first two occurrences are the same line sung twice on the far shore of the Red Sea: “I will sing unto the LORD, for he hath triumphed gloriously: the horse and his rider hath he thrown into the sea” (Exo 15:1), and again from Miriam and the women with timbrels, “Sing ye to the LORD, for he hath triumphed gloriously” (Exo 15:21). Israel had not struck a blow. They had stood still and seen the salvation of the LORD, and the adverb belongs entirely to Him. The third occurrence closes the circle at the end of history: “Then the moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed, when the LORD of hosts shall reign in mount Zion, and in Jerusalem, and before his ancients gloriously” (Isa 24:23). The sun itself is put out of countenance. Between the Red Sea and the reign in Zion the word does not wander into human hands once. That is the doctrine hidden in an adverb: glory is God's manner of acting, and the creature's only proper share in it is the singing. Moses asks the question the word answers: “Who is like unto thee, O LORD, among the gods? who is like thee, glorious in holiness, fearful in praises, doing wonders?” (Exo 15:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines gloriously as in a glorious manner; splendidly; with great renown or dignity; illustriously.
webster_full: GLO'RIOUSLY, adv. [from glorious.]
1. Splendidly; illustriously; with great renown or dignity.
He hath triumphed gloriously.
2. With great honor or magnificence.
The adverb in Scripture is used of the LORD's own acting and reigning, not of the creature's success.
scriptures: Exodus 15:1

Then sang Moses and the children of Israel this song unto the LORD, and spake, saying, I will sing unto the LORD, for he hath triumphed gloriously: the horse and his rider hath he thrown into the sea.
Exodus 15:21
And Miriam answered them, Sing ye to the LORD, for he hath triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider hath he thrown into the sea.
Isaiah 24:23
Then the moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed, when the LORD of hosts shall reign in mount Zion, and in Jerusalem, and before his ancients gloriously.
Exodus 15:11
Who is like unto thee, O LORD, among the gods? who is like thee, glorious in holiness, fearful in praises, doing wonders?
corruption_summary: The adverb has been transferred from God's triumph to man's performance, which is the oldest theft in religion.
corruption_paragraphs: Every age wants the adverb for itself. The nation triumphs gloriously, the ministry grows gloriously, the believer overcomes gloriously. Exodus 15 will not lend the word. Israel's entire contribution at the sea was to be afraid and then to sing. When a church begins to describe its own works with the vocabulary Scripture reserves for God's acts, it has already started down the road to the joyous city of Isaiah 22 — loud, self-congratulating, and unaware of the measuring line.

Isaiah 24:23 supplies the other guard. The sun is ashamed. Whatever glory the creature has is borrowed light, and borrowed light is put out when the Lender appears. This is why the Reformed instinct ends every doctrine at soli Deo gloria: not as a pious signature at the bottom of the page, but as the only honest grammar. Man may sing gloriously of God. He may not triumph gloriously in himself.
roots_summary: Hebrew ga'ah (H1342), to rise up, to be exalted, to triumph; Greek endoxos (G1741), glorious; Latin gloria, renown.
roots_lines: Hebrew ga'oh ga'ah (H1342) — literally rising He has risen, the doubled verb the Authorized Version renders triumphed gloriously; Exodus 15:1.
Hebrew kabod (H3519) — glory, weight, substance; the noun standing behind the adverb's whole idea.
Greek endoxos (G1741) — held in honour, splendid; the Septuagint's word at Exodus 15:11.
Latin gloria — renown, praise; Webster's root, and the last word of the Reformed solas.
Hebrew neged zeqenaw kabod — before his ancients gloriously; Isaiah 24:23, glory shown to the elders of the redeemed.
usage: “He hath triumphed gloriously” — sung by Moses, then by Miriam; the sea did the arguing.
“The moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed” — borrowed light goes out when the Lender reigns.
“Glorious in holiness, fearful in praises” — the holiness is what makes the glory terrible.

pos: adv. (in a sweet manner; agreeably; with pleasantness)
etymology: From sweet, Saxon swete, cognate with Latin suavis. Twice in the Authorized Version, and the two places could not be further apart: a lover's wine and a worm's meal.
biblical_def: The Authorized Version uses sweetly twice, and sets them at opposite ends of the moral world. The Song has it of love and wine: “And the roof of thy mouth like the best wine for my beloved, that goeth down sweetly, causing the lips of those that are asleep to speak” (Son 7:9). Job has it of the grave: “The womb shall forget him; the worm shall feed sweetly on him; he shall be no more remembered; and wickedness shall be broken as a tree” (Job 24:20). One sweetness is covenant love in its proper bed; the other is corruption enjoying a man who spent his life getting away with it. Scripture is not squeamish about this. It will use the tenderest adverb in the language to describe what the worm thinks of the wicked, precisely so the reader will understand that sweetness is not self-authenticating. Something can go down sweetly and be death. The safe sweetness is always the sweetness of God's own word and God's own gift: “More to be desired are they than gold, yea, than much fine gold: sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb” (Psa 19:10); and the sweet sleep of the man who fears the LORD, “thou shalt lie down, and thy sleep shall be sweet” (Pro 3:24).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sweetly as in a sweet manner; with sweetness to the taste; gratefully; with softness or agreeableness.
webster_full: SWEET'LY, adv. [from sweet.]
1. In a sweet manner; gratefully to the taste.
2. Gratefully to the mind or feelings; with softness or agreeableness.
3. With mildness or gentleness of manners.
The Scripture uses it once of wine that goeth down sweetly and once of the worm that feedeth sweetly on the wicked.
scriptures: Song of Solomon 7:9
And the roof of thy mouth like the best wine for my beloved, that goeth down sweetly, causing the lips of those that are asleep to speak.
The womb shall forget him; the worm shall feed sweetly on him; he shall be no more remembered; and wickedness shall be broken as a tree.
Psalm 19:10
More to be desired are they than gold, yea, than much fine gold: sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb.
Proverbs 3:24
When thou liest down, thou shalt not be afraid: yea, thou shalt lie down, and thy sleep shall be sweet.
corruption_summary: Sweetness has been promoted from a quality of God's word to the test of whether a doctrine may be preached.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern rule is that truth must taste sweet before it will be swallowed, and a doctrine that does not is quietly retired: hell, the wrath of God, the narrow gate, headship, the rod. Job 24:20 is the standing answer. The worm feeds sweetly, and nothing is thereby commended. A palate is not a conscience. Psalm 19 gives the believer the one sweetness that may be trusted without qualification — the judgments of the LORD, sweeter than honey precisely where they are hardest.

There is a second and gentler corruption, which is to make sweetly a manner of speech that may never be firm. Ministers are praised for a sweet spirit and rebuked for a plain word, until the pulpit can no longer say what Job said. The Song shows the true place of sweetness: inside covenant, between one man and one woman, where it is a gift and not a governing principle. Outside that, sweetness is a flavour, and flavours have fed the worm before now.
roots_summary: Hebrew meyshariym (H4339), uprightly, smoothly; Hebrew mataq (H4985), to be sweet; Saxon swete; Latin suavis.
roots_lines: Hebrew mataq (H4985) — to be or grow sweet; the root behind the worm that feeds sweetly, Job 24:20.
Hebrew meyshariym (H4339) — straightly, smoothly; the wine of Song 7:9 goes down in uprightness, without catching.
Hebrew 'arab (H6149) — to be pleasant, sweet; used of sleep in Proverbs 3:24 and Jeremiah 31:26.
Hebrew nopheth tsuphiym (H5317) — the honeycomb of Psalm 19:10, the standard the word of God exceeds.
Saxon swete, Latin suavis — Webster's roots, carrying taste and manner together.
usage: “That goeth down sweetly” — covenant love in its own bed, and nowhere else.
“The worm shall feed sweetly on him” — the same adverb, and it is a curse.
“Sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb” — the only sweetness that may be trusted untested.

etymology: From rich, Saxon rice, powerful, wealthy, with the adverbial ending. Twice in the Authorized Version, and both times of what God gives, never of what a man has amassed.
biblical_def: Twice the Authorized Version says richly, and both times God is the giver. The first is the great charge about Scripture in the assembly and the house: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord” (Col 3:16). The word is not to visit; it is to dwell, and to dwell richly — furnished, settled, at home, with room enough to teach and to sing out of. The second is Paul's charge to the wealthy: “Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy” (1Ti 6:17). Riches themselves are uncertain; the God who gives them is not, and He gives richly. Put the two verses together and you have the Reformed doctrine of enjoyment entire: everything is received, nothing is owed, the Giver is trusted rather than the gift, and the proper response is thanksgiving in the name of Christ — “whatsoever ye do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God and the Father by him” (Col 3:17). The adverb rebukes the miser and the ascetic in the same stroke.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines richly as with riches; wealthily; plentifully; abundantly; amply; fully.
webster_full: RICH'LY, adv. [from rich.]
1. With riches; wealthily; splendidly; magnificently; as richly dressed; richly ornamented.
2. Plentifully; abundantly; amply; as he was richly rewarded.
3. Truly; really; abundantly; fully; as a charge richly deserved.
In Scripture the adverb is used of the word of Christ dwelling in the saints and of God giving all things to enjoy.
scriptures: Colossians 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
1 Timothy 6:17
Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy;
Colossians 3:17
And whatsoever ye do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God and the Father by him.
Proverbs 11:28
He that trusteth in his riches shall fall: but the righteous shall flourish as a branch.
corruption_summary: Prosperity teaching reads richly as a promise about the bank; asceticism reads it as an embarrassment. Both miss the Giver.
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity gospel has built a industry on the second half of 1 Timothy 6:17 while cutting the first half out with scissors. The verse does say God giveth us richly all things to enjoy. It says so inside a charge to the rich not to be highminded and not to trust uncertain riches. Lift the clause out of its warning and you have manufactured the exact sin Paul is warning against. The same chapter ends with laying up a good foundation against the time to come, which is not a portfolio.

The opposite corruption is quieter and more respectable: a suspicion that enjoyment itself is worldly, that the sober Christian should receive God's gifts with a wince. Colossians 3:16 will not have it. The word dwelling richly produces singing. The Reformed tradition has always held both ends — creation is good, gratitude is the proper posture, and the heart that trusts the branch rather than the Root shall fall (Pro 11:28). Riches are a stewardship, not a shame and not a wage.
roots_summary: Greek plousios (G4146), richly, abundantly; enoikeo (G1774), to dwell in as a house; Saxon rice, powerful.
roots_lines: Greek plousios (G4146) — adverb, richly, abundantly; the same stem in both Colossians 3:16 and 1 Timothy 6:17.
Greek enoikeito (G1774) — let it dwell in, inhabit as a house; the word of Christ takes up residence, it does not call.
Greek apolausis (G619) — enjoyment; 1 Timothy 6:17 gives all things eis apolausin, for enjoying.
Greek hupselophronein (G5309) — to be highminded; the sin the rich are charged against in the same breath.
Saxon rice — powerful, wealthy; Webster's root, where riches and rule share one word.
usage: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly” — a resident, furnished, with room to sing.
“Who giveth us richly all things to enjoy” — read with the warning it is attached to.
“He that trusteth in his riches shall fall” — the branch flourishes because of the Root.

pos: adv. (in a wonderful manner; marvellously; so as to excite wonder)
etymology: From wondrous, from wonder, Saxon wundor, a marvel. Twice in the Authorized Version, and in both places the wonder is a work of God that men stand still and watch.
biblical_def: Both occurrences of wondrously put God at the working end of the verb and men at the watching end. The first is at Manoah's rock: “So Manoah took a kid with a meat offering, and offered it upon a rock unto the LORD: and the angel did wondrously; and Manoah and his wife looked on” (Jdg 13:19). The angel ascends in the altar flame; the parents of Samson fall on their faces. Nothing is asked of them but sacrifice and sight. The second is Joel's promise after the locust years: “And ye shall eat in plenty, and be satisfied, and praise the name of the LORD your God, that hath dealt wondrously with you: and my people shall never be ashamed” (Joe 2:26). The wonder there is restoration — the years the locust hath eaten given back. So the word covers both ends of God's dealing: the blaze that goes up from the rock, and the slow refilling of a stripped land. Both are wonders; only one is spectacular. The Psalter keeps the same balance, ascribing all of it to God alone — “Blessed be the LORD God, the God of Israel, who only doeth wondrous things” (Psa 72:18) — and finding the wonder in the body as readily as in the fire: “I am fearfully and wonderfully made” (Psa 139:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines wondrously as in a wonderful manner; to a wonderful degree; so as to excite astonishment.
webster_full: WON'DROUSLY, adv. [from wondrous.]
In a wonderful manner; to a degree or in a manner to excite astonishment or admiration.
Chloe complains, and wondrously's aggriev'd.
The Scripture uses it of the angel at Manoah's rock and of the LORD's restoring of the locust years.
scriptures: Judges 13:19
So Manoah took a kid with a meat offering, and offered it upon a rock unto the LORD: and the angel did wondrously; and Manoah and his wife looked on.
Joel 2:26
And ye shall eat in plenty, and be satisfied, and praise the name of the LORD your God, that hath dealt wondrously with you: and my people shall never be ashamed.
Psalm 72:18
Blessed be the LORD God, the God of Israel, who only doeth wondrous things.
Psalm 139:14
I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well.
corruption_summary: Wonder has been handed to the sign-seeker on one side and explained away by the naturalist on the other.
corruption_paragraphs: The charismatic movement has taught a generation to hunt the Manoah moment and to count an ordinary providence as no dealing at all. Joel 2:26 is the corrective: God deals wondrously in harvests. A congregation trained to look only for fire on the rock will walk through twenty years of answered prayer, filled barns, and converted children and call it a dry season. Psalm 72:18 says He only doeth wondrous things, and it does not limit the catalogue to the spectacular.

The naturalist commits the opposite error with better manners. Everything is mechanism; wonder is a feeling produced by ignorance and dissolved by explanation. Psalm 139:14 answers from inside the body: the more the frame is understood, the more fearfully and wonderfully made it is proved to be. Explanation is not the enemy of wonder; it is the inventory of it. The man who can describe the eye and not worship has not been made wiser, only louder.
roots_summary: Hebrew pala' (H6381), to be marvellous, to do wonderfully; Greek thaumasios (G2297), wonderful; Saxon wundor, a marvel.
roots_lines: Hebrew pala' (H6381) — to be extraordinary, beyond the doing of men; the verb at Judges 13:19 and Joel 2:26.
Hebrew pele' (H6382) — a wonder; the noun in Isaiah 9:6, where the Child's name begins Wonderful.
Hebrew niphla'oth (H6381) — wondrous works; the standing Psalter word for God's acts in history.
Greek thaumasios (G2297) — wonderful, marvellous; Matthew 21:15 of the things Christ did in the temple.
Saxon wundor — a marvel, a portent; Webster's root, still audible in the English.
usage: “The angel did wondrously; and Manoah and his wife looked on” — sacrifice, then sight.
“Hath dealt wondrously with you” — said of a harvest, not a miracle.
“Who only doeth wondrous things” — the adverb has one subject.

pos: a. (lovely; worthy of love; deserving of affection)
etymology: French aimable, from Latin amabilis, lovable, from amare, to love. A single occurrence in the Authorized Version, and it is spent on the house of God.
biblical_def: The word occurs once in all of Scripture, and the sons of Korah spend it on the tabernacle: “How amiable are thy tabernacles, O LORD of hosts!” (Psa 84:1). The English has softened since 1611; today amiable means pleasant company, and a man is called amiable when he is easy to sit beside. In the Authorized Version it carries its full Latin weight — amabilis, lovable, worthy to be loved. The psalmist is not saying the courts are agreeable. He is saying they are the most desirable place in the world, and the next verse proves how far he means it: “My soul longeth, yea, even fainteth for the courts of the LORD: my heart and my flesh crieth out for the living God” (Psa 84:2). This is homesickness for a building because of who dwells in it. He would rather keep the door there than own the tents of the wicked: “I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness” (Psa 84:10). David says the same thing as a single request: “One thing have I desired of the LORD… that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the LORD” (Psa 27:4). The public assembly of God's people is the amiable place, and a Christian who has lost that affection has lost something the Psalter assumes.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines amiable as lovely; worthy of love; deserving of affection; and applied to things, as an amiable temper or amiable manners.
webster_full: A'MIABLE, a. [Fr. aimable; L. amabilis, from amo, to love.]
1. Lovely; worthy of love; deserving of affection; applied usually to persons.
But it is applied to things also; as amiable manners, an amiable temper.
2. Pretending or showing love.
How amiable are thy tabernacles, O LORD of hosts. Ps. 84.
scriptures: Psalm 84:1
To the chief Musician upon Gittith, A Psalm for the sons of Korah. How amiable are thy tabernacles, O LORD of hosts!
Psalm 84:2
My soul longeth, yea, even fainteth for the courts of the LORD: my heart and my flesh crieth out for the living God.
Psalm 84:10
For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness.
Psalm 27:4
One thing have I desired of the LORD, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the LORD, and to enquire in his temple.
corruption_summary: The word has faded from worthy of love to easy to get along with, and the affection it once described has faded with it.
corruption_paragraphs: The drift in the English is a parable of the drift in the church. Amiable now means agreeable, and the compliment is paid to a man who causes no trouble. So the congregation is graded on friendliness, the minister on approachability, and the worship on whether newcomers found it pleasant. Psalm 84 is doing something else entirely. The tabernacles are lovable because the LORD of hosts is there, and the psalmist faints for them. Pleasantness is a by-product; presence is the point.

There is a practical corruption downstream. If the assembly is merely agreeable, attendance becomes optional, a preference among weekend goods, and a man reasons that he can love God at home. The Psalter grants no such arrangement: a day in the courts is better than a thousand elsewhere, and the doorkeeper's post beats the householder's tent among the wicked. The regulative principle exists to guard this — that what is done in the courts is what God commanded, so that the amiable place stays His house and does not quietly become ours.
roots_summary: Hebrew yedidoth (H3039), beloved, lovely; Latin amabilis, from amare, to love; French aimable.
roots_lines: Hebrew yedidoth (H3039) — beloved things, lovely places; the plural of the same root that names Solomon Jedidiah, beloved of the LORD.
Hebrew mishkenoth (H4908) — dwelling places, tabernacles; the plural is intensive, the whole sanctuary complex.
Latin amabilis, from amare — able to be loved; Webster's root, still the exact sense of Psalm 84:1.
Hebrew kasaph (H3700) — to long, to pine; Psalm 84:2, the soul fainting for the courts.
Hebrew histophep (H5605) — to stand at the threshold; the doorkeeper of Psalm 84:10, a post, not a demotion.
usage: “How amiable are thy tabernacles” — lovable, not merely pleasant.
“My soul longeth, yea, even fainteth” — the measure of how strong the word is.
“Rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God” — the threshold beats the tent.

pos: adv. (in a quiet manner; without noise or agitation; peaceably)
etymology: From quiet, Latin quietus, at rest, from quiescere, to rest. Twice in the Authorized Version, once of a murder and once of the soul waiting for salvation.
biblical_def: The Authorized Version gives quietly two uses, and they are a warning and a rule. The warning is Joab: “And when Abner was returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside in the gate to speak with him quietly, and smote him there under the fifth rib” (2Sa 3:27). Quietness here is the cover of a murder — a lowered voice used to get a man close enough to kill. The rule is Jeremiah in the ashes of the city: “It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD” (Lam 3:26). That is the posture the whole Bible commends to the afflicted: not a stoic numbness, and not the busy self-rescue that will not sit still, but hope and silence together, waiting for a salvation that is God's to bring. Isaiah puts the same doctrine as a rebuke to a nation that preferred cavalry: “In returning and rest shall ye be saved; in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength: and ye would not” (Isa 30:15). And Paul makes it an ordinary Christian ambition rather than a mystic state: “that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands” (1Th 4:11). Quietness in Scripture is industrious, ordinary, and directed at God — and it is never a tone of voice used to get near a man.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines quietly as in a quiet state; without motion; without tumult, alarm, dispute or disturbance; peaceably; calmly; patiently.
webster_full: QUI'ETLY, adv. [from quiet.]
1. In a quiet state; without motion; as, to lie or sit quietly.
2. Without tumult, alarm, dispute or disturbance; peaceably; as, to live quietly.
3. Calmly; without agitation or violent emotion; patiently; as, to submit quietly to unavoidable evils.
It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD. Lam. 3.
scriptures: Lamentations 3:26
It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD.
2 Samuel 3:27
And when Abner was returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside in the gate to speak with him quietly, and smote him there under the fifth rib, that he died, for the blood of Asahel his brother.
Isaiah 30:15
For thus saith the Lord GOD, the Holy One of Israel; In returning and rest shall ye be saved; in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength: and ye would not.
1 Thessalonians 4:11
And that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands, as we commanded you;
corruption_summary: Quietness has been repackaged as a technique for calming the self rather than a posture of waiting on God.
corruption_paragraphs: The contemplative-and-mindfulness industry has borrowed the Bible's vocabulary of stillness and emptied it of its object. Quiet becomes a method: still the mind, observe the breath, detach from the thought. Lamentations 3:26 is doing the reverse. The soul is not emptied; it is aimed. A man hopes and quietly waits, and what he waits for is named — the salvation of the LORD. Remove the object and what is left is not Christian quietness but a technique that works about as well on a pagan.

The second corruption is political rather than devotional. Isaiah's generation would not have quietness and confidence because those looked like doing nothing while Assyria marched. Every anxious age repeats the calculation. But 1 Thessalonians 4:11 shows quietness is not idleness — it is minding your own business and working with your hands, which is the least fashionable form of courage there is. And Joab stands at the other edge as a permanent caution: a quiet voice is not evidence of a quiet heart.
roots_summary: Hebrew dumam (H1748), silently, in stillness; Greek hesuchazo (G2270), to be still; Latin quietus, at rest.
roots_lines: Hebrew dumam (H1748) — in silence, still; Lamentations 3:26, the waiting that makes no noise but has an object.
Hebrew shalom (H7965) rendered quietly at 2 Samuel 3:27 — Joab spoke in peace, which is the horror of the verse.
Hebrew shaqat (H8252) — to be quiet, undisturbed; the land had rest forty years in Judges.
Greek hesuchazein (G2270) — to be still, to keep quiet; 1 Thessalonians 4:11, a thing to be studied.
Latin quietus, from quiescere — to rest; Webster's root, and the source of English acquiesce.
usage: “Hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD” — hope is half of it; the object is the other half.
“In quietness and in confidence shall be your strength: and ye would not” — the refusal is the sin.
“Study to be quiet, and to do your own business” — quietness with calluses on it.

pos: a. (giving comfort; strengthening; in the Authorized Version, of words that put heart into a man)
etymology: From comfort, Old French conforter, from Latin confortare, to strengthen greatly, from con- and fortis, strong. The root is strength, not ease — a fact the modern English has entirely lost.
biblical_def: Modern English hears comfortable and thinks of a chair. The Authorized Version means something with a spine in it: confortare, to make strong. Both occurrences are about speech. The woman of Tekoah tells David, “The word of my lord the king shall now be comfortable: for as an angel of God, so is my lord the king to discern good and bad” (2Sa 14:17) — a king's ruling is comfortable because it is discerning and settles the matter. And the LORD answers the interceding angel “with good words and comfortable words” (Zec 1:13) after seventy years of silence over a ruined Jerusalem. In neither place is anyone made cosy. They are made strong. This is why the great comfort passages of Scripture are full of hard facts rather than soothing feelings: “Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God” (Isa 40:1) opens a chapter about grass withering and the word of God standing for ever. And Paul roots all Christian consolation in God Himself, “who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble” (2Co 1:4). Comfort in Scripture is not the removal of the trouble; it is strength supplied inside it, and the strength comes by words.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines comfortable as being in a state of ease or moderate enjoyment; and also, giving comfort, administering comfort or consolation — a comfortable word being one that strengthens.
webster_full: COM'FORTABLE, a. [See Comfort.]
1. Being in a state of ease, or moderate enjoyment; as a comfortable situation.
2. Admitting comfort; that may afford comfort.
3. Giving comfort; affording consolation; as comfortable words.
Let thy merciful kindness be for my comfort. The Latin confortare is to strengthen greatly, from fortis, strong.
scriptures: 2 Samuel 14:17
Then thine handmaid said, The word of my lord the king shall now be comfortable: for as an angel of God, so is my lord the king to discern good and bad: therefore the LORD thy God will be with thee.
Zechariah 1:13
And the LORD answered the angel that talked with me with good words and comfortable words.
Isaiah 40:1
Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God.
2 Corinthians 1:4
Who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God.
corruption_summary: Comfort has migrated from strength-supplied to distress-avoided, and the church has followed the word down.
corruption_paragraphs: Once comfortable means unbothered, a comfortable church is one where nothing is said that would trouble anybody, and comfort ministry becomes the management of feeling. The Latin root judges the whole arrangement: confortare, to strengthen greatly. Zechariah's comfortable words were spoken over rubble and promised that the LORD would yet choose Jerusalem. They did not clear away one stone that morning. They put iron into men who had to keep building.

The therapeutic register makes this worse by reclassifying affliction as damage to be processed rather than a providence to be borne under God. Where Scripture says tribulation, the new vocabulary says trauma; where Scripture supplies strength, the new vocabulary supplies validation. 2 Corinthians 1:4 gives the true chain and it runs the other way: God comforts us in tribulation so that we may comfort others — the affliction is not wasted, and the comfort is transferable because it was never a mood. It was strength, and strength can be passed on.
roots_summary: Latin confortare, to strengthen greatly, from fortis, strong; Hebrew tob (H2896), good; Greek parakaleo (G3870), to call alongside.
roots_lines: Latin confortare, from con- and fortis — to strengthen greatly; the buried root, and the whole doctrine in one word.
Hebrew dabarim tobim dabarim nihumim — good words, comfortable words; Zechariah 1:13, spoken over ruins.
Greek parakaleo (G3870) — to call to one's side, to exhort, to comfort; the verb behind 2 Corinthians 1:4.
Greek paraklesis (G3874) — consolation, encouragement; the noun, and cousin to the Comforter of John 14:16.
Hebrew nacham (H5162) — to sigh, then to console; the word that opens Isaiah 40:1.
usage: “Good words and comfortable words” — spoken over rubble, and they built.
“Comfort ye, comfort ye my people” — and then forty verses about grass withering.
“The comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God” — strength that can be handed on.

pos: a. (rich; having large possessions; and in the Authorized Version, of a place of abundance and security)
etymology: From wealth, Saxon wela, weal, welfare, prosperity — the older English sense being well-being generally, of which money is only one part.
biblical_def: Both occurrences of wealthy in the Authorized Version describe a place, not a person, and they land on opposite sides of the ledger. The first is deliverance: “Thou hast caused men to ride over our heads; we went through fire and through water: but thou broughtest us out into a wealthy place” (Psa 66:12). The wealthy place is what lies on the far side of the fire and the water; it is the end of a providence, not an escape from one. The second is indictment: “Arise, get you up unto the wealthy nation, that dwelleth without care, saith the LORD, which have neither gates nor bars, which dwell alone” (Jer 49:31). Kedar is wealthy and careless, unwalled because it fears nothing, and the LORD is sending Nebuchadrezzar to it. Put the two together and the doctrine is plain: wealth as God's gift at the end of a trial is a mercy to be sung about; wealth as a settled condition that removes the sense of need is a summons. Proverbs keeps the same edge on both sides — “He that trusteth in his riches shall fall: but the righteous shall flourish as a branch” (Pro 11:28) — and warns that the accounts are not what they look like: “There is that maketh himself rich, yet hath nothing: there is that maketh himself poor, yet hath great riches” (Pro 13:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines wealthy as rich; having large possessions in lands, goods, money or securities; opulent; affluent.
webster_full: WEALTH'Y, a. welth'y. [from wealth.]
1. Rich; having large possessions in lands, goods, money or securities, or larger than the generality of men; opulent; affluent.
It is often synonymous with rich, but rich may denote a greater degree of opulence.
2. Abundant; ample; as a wealthy place.
Thou broughtest us out into a wealthy place. Ps. 66.
scriptures: Psalm 66:12
Thou hast caused men to ride over our heads; we went through fire and through water: but thou broughtest us out into a wealthy place.
Jeremiah 49:31
Arise, get you up unto the wealthy nation, that dwelleth without care, saith the LORD, which have neither gates nor bars, which dwell alone.
Proverbs 11:28
He that trusteth in his riches shall fall: but the righteous shall flourish as a branch.
Proverbs 13:7
There is that maketh himself rich, yet hath nothing: there is that maketh himself poor, yet hath great riches.
corruption_summary: Prosperity preaching claims Psalm 66:12 and skips the fire and the water; the ascetic claims Jeremiah 49:31 and forgets it was carelessness, not wealth, that was judged.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 66:12 is a favourite verse of prosperity teaching, always quoted from the comma forward. The whole verse has men riding over the psalmist's head, and fire, and water, and only then the wealthy place — and God is the subject of every clause including the riding. A promise of the destination that suppresses the road is not the psalm; it is an advertisement using the psalm's words. Job, Joseph, and Paul all reached wealthy places by exactly this route, and none of them could have sold tickets for it.

The opposite error treats Jeremiah 49:31 as a verdict on money itself. Read it again: the charge against Kedar is dwelling without care, with neither gates nor bars, alone — a security so complete it has stopped looking up. That is a condition of soul available at any income. The Reformed doctrine of vocation holds that wealth is a stewardship with an account to render, that trusting it is the fall (Pro 11:28), and that the books as men keep them are frequently the reverse of the books as God keeps them (Pro 13:7).
roots_summary: Hebrew revayah (H7310), abundance, saturation; Hebrew shalev (H7961), at ease, careless; Saxon wela, weal, welfare.
roots_lines: Hebrew revayah (H7310) — overflowing abundance, saturation; the wealthy place of Psalm 66:12, a watered land after fire.
Hebrew shalev (H7961) — quiet, at ease, careless; the wealthy nation of Jeremiah 49:31, and the word carries the rebuke.
Saxon wela — weal, well-being; the older English in which wealth meant welfare and not only money.
Hebrew hon (H1952) — substance, riches; the noun in Proverbs 11:28 and 13:7.
Greek euporia (G2142) — wealth, plenty; Acts 19:25, where a craft's wealth resists the gospel.
usage: “Through fire and through water… into a wealthy place” — the road is part of the promise.
“The wealthy nation, that dwelleth without care” — unwalled, unafraid, and summoned.
“Maketh himself poor, yet hath great riches” — the ledgers do not agree.

etymology: From plenteous, from Old French plentiveus, from Latin plenitas, fulness, from plenus, full. Twice in the Authorized Version: once of Egypt's seven good years, once of the reward of diligence.
biblical_def: The word names abundance, and Scripture uses it twice with a very deliberate difference. The first is Joseph's Egypt: “And the seven years of plenteousness, that was in the land of Egypt, were ended” (Gen 41:53). That plenteousness was pure gift — “in the seven plenteous years the earth brought forth by handfuls” (Gen 41:47) — foretold by God, unearned by Egypt, and its whole purpose was to be stored against the famine that was coming. Plenty in Scripture is frequently a preparation rather than a reward. The second use is Solomon's: “The thoughts of the diligent tend only to plenteousness; but of every one that is hasty only to want” (Pro 21:5). Here abundance is the ordinary end of steady, thoughtful labour, and haste is named as the road to poverty. So the two texts guard each other. Genesis forbids the diligent man from imagining he made his own harvest; Proverbs forbids the idle man from calling his want a providence. And behind both stands the attribute the Psalter keeps returning to, that the plenteousness is first of all in God Himself and is mercy before it is grain: “For thou, Lord, art good, and ready to forgive; and plenteous in mercy unto all them that call upon thee” (Psa 86:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines plenteousness as abundance; plenty; a full or adequate supply; sufficiency.
webster_full: PLEN'TEOUSNESS, n. [from plenteous.]
1. Abundance; plenty; a full or adequate supply; sufficiency.
In the seven plenteous years, the earth brought forth by handfuls. Gen. 41.
2. Fertility; fruitfulness; as the plenteousness of a season.
The thoughts of the diligent tend only to plenteousness. Prov. 21.
scriptures: Genesis 41:53
And the seven years of plenteousness, that was in the land of Egypt, were ended.
Proverbs 21:5
The thoughts of the diligent tend only to plenteousness; but of every one that is hasty only to want.
Genesis 41:47
And in the seven plenteous years the earth brought forth by handfuls.
Psalm 86:5
For thou, Lord, art good, and ready to forgive; and plenteous in mercy unto all them that call upon thee.
corruption_summary: Plenty is treated as a verdict on the man who has it, which flatters the full and condemns the hungry.
corruption_paragraphs: Both halves of the age make the same mistake in opposite directions. One says abundance proves God's favour, so the full man is approved and the empty man is under a cloud. The other says abundance proves theft, so the full man is guilty by arithmetic. Genesis 41 refuses both. Egypt's seven years of plenteousness were given to a pagan nation for the sake of a famine none of them yet believed in, and the man who read them rightly was a Hebrew slave out of a prison. Plenty proved nothing about Egypt's virtue; it proved something about God's foresight.

Proverbs 21:5 then blocks the fatalism that would follow. If plenty is only ever a sovereign gift, a man might conclude his own habits are irrelevant. Solomon says the thoughts of the diligent tend to plenteousness and haste to want — means are real, laziness is culpable, and a Christian doctrine of providence that dissolves the duty of work has stopped being the Bible's. God is plenteous in mercy (Psa 86:5); He is not thereby indulgent toward sloth.
roots_summary: Hebrew sava' (H7647), plenty, satiety; Hebrew mothar (H4195), profit, abundance; Latin plenus, full.
roots_lines: Hebrew sava' (H7647) — plenty, satiety; the seven years of Genesis 41:53, named before they arrived.
Hebrew mothar (H4195) — advantage, profit, surplus; the plenteousness diligence tends to in Proverbs 21:5.
Hebrew rav-chesed (H7227, H2617) — plenteous in mercy, Psalm 86:5; the abundance that is in God before it is in the field.
Latin plenus, plenitas — full, fulness; Webster's root through Old French plentiveus.
Hebrew qomets — by handfuls; Genesis 41:47, the harvest so heavy it is measured by the fist.
usage: “The seven years of plenteousness… were ended” — plenty has a term, and it was always for the famine.
“The thoughts of the diligent tend only to plenteousness” — thought first, then diligence, then plenty.
“Plenteous in mercy unto all them that call” — the abundance is His before it is ours.
